text: The report works in Power BI Desktop. But the Southeast manager doesn't have Power BI Desktop open, and shouldn't need it. This lesson gets the report from your machine into the Power BI Service, where it opens in a browser.

Publishing takes four steps. From the Home ribbon in Power BI Desktop, click Publish. Choose a destination workspace — a shared workspace for Carraway's BI team, not My Workspace, since My Workspace can't be shared with anyone else. Power BI uploads both the report and the dataset together. And once it's done, a confirmation link opens the report directly in the browser.

Worth understanding: that one pbix file becomes two separate objects in the Service. The dataset holds the data model — the tables, the relationships, the three DAX measures — and it's the dataset that has refresh settings. The report holds the actual pages and visuals a viewer sees. Different objects, same source file.

For sharing, this project calls for something simple: direct sharing with one stakeholder's email, not a full Power BI App. An App is built for distributing multiple reports to multiple audiences — useful once that structure exists, but over-engineering for a single Monday-call report.

In the Service, open the report and click Share. Enter the stakeholder's work email, and confirm they have at least Viewer access to the workspace. That access matters — without it, the link opens an access request screen instead of the report itself.

The report is published and shared. Next lesson is the one that actually matters most to the stakeholder — how to walk them through this dashboard in about two minutes, leading with the answer to their real question instead of touring every visual.
